title: Trace breadth-first search without guessing
goal: Use a queue and a seen set to explain a small graph traversal and avoid duplicate work.

sources.title: Original illustrative example
sources.location: Authored demo; not a real course, assessment or financial forecast.

scenes.title: Explore one layer at a time

cues.text: Imagine finding the fewest links from A to every other node in an unweighted graph. Breadth first search explores nearby nodes before farther ones.
A queue gives first in, first out behavior. A newly discovered node waits behind the nodes already in that queue.
A seen set records discoveries. We mark a node when we enqueue it, so another path cannot add the same node again.

steps.title: Explore by distance
steps.body: Finish the nearer layer before the next one.

steps.title: Mark on enqueue
steps.body: Record a discovery immediately to prevent duplicate work.

cues.text: Start with A in the queue and in the seen set. In this example A lists B before C in its neighbor list.
Remove A and discover B. Mark B as seen and append it to the queue. B is one edge away from A.
Then discover C from A and append C after B. The queue is now B followed by C; both are in the first layer.
Next remove B and discover D. Append D behind C, so C will be processed before the second layer node D.

scenes.title: Connect the picture to the code

cues.text: The left removal operation takes the oldest queued node. This is the line that gives the traversal its breadth first order.
For each outgoing neighbor, test whether it is absent from seen. When C later reaches D, this test will be false.
Mark a new neighbor before appending it. Otherwise, two nodes in the current layer could both schedule the same future node.
Appending places new work behind existing work. The loop continues until the queue is empty; no recursive call is needed.

steps.note: Remove from the front: oldest queued node first.
D is skipped when another path has already discovered it.
Mark the discovery before scheduling it.
Append at the back; preserve the layer order.

scenes.title: Three details that change the result

cues.text: If we mark only when removing a node, duplicate entries can accumulate. Marking on enqueue avoids that unnecessary work.
If we remove from the back instead, we are using a stack. That changes the strategy and loses the usual breadth first distance guarantee.
The exact order within one layer depends on neighbor order. Shortest path distances still agree for this unweighted graph.

steps.title: Seen means discovered
steps.body: Do not wait until processing to record it.

steps.title: Queue is not a stack
steps.body: Remove from the front, not the back.

steps.title: Neighbor order matters
steps.body: B before C is an input choice, not a universal rule.

scenes.title: What if A lists C before B?

cues.text: Keep the graph, but list C before B in A’s neighbors. Predict the processing order before following the trace.
A is first. C enters the queue before B, so C is processed next and discovers D.
B was already queued before D. Process B next; its neighbor D is already seen, so do not enqueue D again.
D is last. The processing order is A, C, B, D. D is still two edges from A; only the tie within the first layer changed.

steps.note: Process A; enqueue C, then B.
Process C; enqueue D behind B.
Process B; D is already seen.
Process D. Order: A, C, B, D.

check.question: Why does D not get enqueued twice?
check.answer: The seen set is updated when D is first enqueued. The second path finds it already seen and skips it.

scenes.title: Read the state, not just the arrows

cues.text: At every step, keep track of the current node, the queue in order, and the set of discovered nodes.
Use the code to justify each state change. Remove the oldest item, examine neighbors, then mark and append only new discoveries.
That is the reusable pattern: a queue controls the order, while the seen set prevents repeated work.

steps.title: Queue
steps.body: The ordered list of work waiting to be processed.

steps.title: Seen set
steps.body: Every node discovered so far, including queued nodes.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body: A record of why each update follows from the code.
